system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2119-06-17 19:13:00 to 2119-06-23 16:49:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with chest pain, nausea, and vomiting following a dialysis session. Initial concerns for cardiac ischemia were ruled out as troponin levels were mildly elevated but stable and MB negative, with EKG changes attributed to lead placement. A urinary tract infection was diagnosed based on urinalysis and symptoms of dysuria, and treated with cefepime initially, then transitioned to ciprofloxacin. Two painful skin lesions on the inner thigh and left hip were biopsied, confirming calciphylaxis, leading to initiation of sodium thiosulfate therapy and increased dialysis frequency to daily, then planned for four times weekly. Nausea was managed by switching from calcium acetate to lanthanum as a phosphate binder and using antiemetics. Hypertension was addressed with uptitration of isosorbide dinitrate and addition of amlodipine. The chronic abdominal wound showed signs of healing and was deemed stable. The patient was discharged to an extended care facility with plans for ongoing dialysis, dermatology follow-up, and management of multiple comorbidities.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with ESRD unable to get dialysis with her

ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
75 mcg of fentanyl and 15 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 25 min during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.

MEDICATIONS: Fentanyl, Versed, lidocaine, 10 mg of hydralazine.

CONTRAST: 20 ml of Optiray contrast.

FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  6.8 min, 48 mGy

PROCEDURE:  PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the explanation of the risks,
benefits and alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was
obtained from the patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography
suite and placed supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was
performed per ___ protocol. The right/left, upper chest/groin was prepped
and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

A scout fluoroscopic image demonstrated a left internal jugular approach
hemodialysis catheter in good position. Subsequent contrast injection into
both ports demonstrated lingering contrast around the catheter tip suggestive
of a fibrin sheath. A super stiff glidewire was passed into a single port. The
indwelling tunneled catheter was removed over the wire with assistance of
blunt dissection. A 7 ___ 25 cm by tip sheath was advanced along the
glidewire to the SVC -brachiocephalic junction.  Hand injection of dilute
contrast demonstrated brisk contrast flow into the right atrium. An 8 mm x 4
cm x 80 ___ balloon was advanced along the glidewire into the upper
right atrium.  Serial balloon dilatations were done along the presumed course
of the prior hemodialysis catheter. No waist was identified to suggest
residual fibrin sheath. The balloon catheter was deflated and removed over the
wire. The 7 ___ sheath was advanced into the cephalad inferior vena cava. A
second superstiff glidewire was advanced through the sheath into the inferior
vena cava. The sheath was withdrawn and the 15.5 ___ 24 cm tunneled
dialysis catheter was advanced along the parallel wires with tip terminating
in the right atrium.

The skin incision site was closed with a ___ Vicryl subcuticular pursestring
suture. The catheter was sutured in place with 0 silk sutures. Final spot
fluoroscopic image demonstrating good alignment of the catheter and no
kinking. The tip is in the right atrium. The catheter was flushed and both
lumens were capped. Sterile dressings were applied. The patient tolerated the
procedure well.

FINDINGS: 

Suggestion of fibrin sheath surrounding the indwelling hemodialysis catheter.
Successful exchange of hemodialysis catheter with final fluoroscopic image
showing 15.5 ___ hemodialysis catheter with tip terminating in the right
atrium.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a left internal jugular approach 19cm tip-to-cuff
length tunneled dialysis line.  The tip of the catheter terminates in the
right atrium. The catheter is ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___. I understand your dialysis line wasn’t working—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I went for dialysis four days ago, but they couldn’t use my line. They replaced it this morning, but it still didn’t work when I got back to dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve reviewed your labs and imaging. There was a fibrin sheath around the old catheter, which likely caused the blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A what sheath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A fibrin sheath—it’s like a thin layer of clot that can form around the catheter and block blood flow. We tried using tPA to dissolve it, but it didn’t work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a new catheter tomorrow. The radiology team will do it under imaging guidance to make sure it’s positioned correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it work this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful. We’ll also use a balloon to clear any remaining blockage in the vein. Most patients do well after this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, you mentioned left heel pain—how long has that been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About four weeks. No injury, just constant ache. It’s worse when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get an X-ray to rule out a fracture. Given your history, it could be plantar fasciitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s inflammation in the tissue along the bottom of your foot. Common in people with diabetes and kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your X-ray showed no fracture, but there’s thickening of the plantar fascia—consistent with plantar fasciitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no break, just inflammation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll manage it with rest, pain meds, and possibly physical therapy later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now, about your dialysis line—we placed a new one this morning. It’s a split-tip catheter, designed to reduce clotting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And it’s working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the flow is good. You’ll have dialysis later today, and we’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count was elevated when you came in—13.4. It’s now down to 8.5, which is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was I infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The dermatology team looked at your thigh wounds—those from your calciphylaxis—and noticed pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, those are so painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They took a deep culture. It grew several bacteria, including Pseudomonas, which can be serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudomonas? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially in wounds. But your culture showed it’s sensitive to ciprofloxacin, so we’re treating it with cipro and clindamycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ten days total. You’ve started today, so you’ll finish after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also got your PTH level from your outside records—it’s very high, 1110.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means you have severe hyperparathyroidism. That’s likely driving your calciphylaxis—those painful skin lesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Surgery to remove your parathyroid glands—parathyroidectomy—is the best option. Dermatology recommended it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But without it, the calciphylaxis will keep getting worse. You’ll follow up with the surgeon after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll go. But I don’t want those injections they mentioned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mean the intralesional sodium thiosulfate? That’s okay—you refused, and we respect that. We’ll focus on the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wounds are being cared for by the wound team. They’re changing the dressings regularly and packing them properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They hurt so much when they change them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’ll give you pain meds before each change. It’s important to keep the wounds clean to prevent more infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Your dialysis is working, your infection is responding, and your pain is better controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to an extended care facility. You’ll continue dialysis there and finish your antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see Dr. ___ next week to discuss parathyroidectomy. That’s the next big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to discharge. Your new catheter is working well, and your wounds are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take cipro and clindamycin for ten days, plus your other meds like cinacalcet and sevelamer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep the dressings clean. The facility will help you with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll go to the surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll be following up with your sister to make sure everything goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s been so helpful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Take care, Ms. ___. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your heel pain should improve with rest. Avoid standing too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And call if the pain worsens or you develop redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the transport team will take you shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted due to malfunction of her hemodialysis catheter, which failed despite initial replacement and tPA treatment. A new tunneled catheter was successfully placed, restoring dialysis access. During admission, she was found to have infected calciphylaxis wounds with polymicrobial growth including Pseudomonas, prompting a 10-day course of ciprofloxacin and clindamycin. Her severe hyperparathyroidism (PTH 1110) was confirmed as a driver of calciphylaxis, and she was scheduled for surgical evaluation for parathyroidectomy. Left heel pain was evaluated with X-ray, showing no fracture but findings consistent with plantar fasciitis. She was discharged to an extended care facility on antibiotics and with wound care instructions, to continue dialysis and follow up with surgery.
